conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your transplant surgeons. We’re about to take you to surgery for your kidney transplant today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ve been waiting a long time for this. Is everything ready?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, everything’s set. We’ll be using a deceased donor pediatric en bloc transplant, which means two small kidneys will be placed together. We expect good function, but there may be some challenges due to your prior surgeries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time I was in for that cough, they were worried about infection. Is that still a concern?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Your recent illness was viral, not bacterial, and your blood cultures were negative. We stopped antibiotics before this admission. We’ll monitor closely, but you’re cleared for surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. The transplant surgery went through, but it was complex. There was a lot of scar tissue, and we had to transfuse platelets due to oozing during the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that sounds rough. Are the kidneys working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Urine output is low right now, which we call slow graft function. It’s common, especially with pediatric kidneys. We’re giving IV fluids and Lasix to help. Your creatinine was 8.4 on admission—we’ll watch for it to come down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the liver biopsy you mentioned? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The liver looked firm and nodular, so we took a biopsy. Results aren’t back yet, but we’re checking for hepatitis and other issues. We’ll get Hepatology involved if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your renal ultrasound shows both kidneys have good blood flow. No blockage or leaks. That’s excellent news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My belly feels swollen though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw some ascites—fluid in the abdomen. It could be from heart or liver issues. We’ll monitor it. Your JP drain is collecting fluid, and we tested it—no leak from the kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: HBV testing came back: you’re positive for core and surface antibodies, meaning past exposure. No active virus detected. But we’ll start Lamivudine to prevent reactivation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that affect my transplant?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s preventive. Hepatitis B can reactivate under immunosuppression. This protects your liver and transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine dropped to 2.0, and urine output is improving. That’s a great sign your kidneys are waking up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But I’ve been short of breath. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. You’re showing signs of volume overload. Cardiology is coming to evaluate. Your heart function has been reduced, and the extra fluid may be stressing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The echo shows your heart is working at 40-45% and you have moderate pulmonary hypertension. Atrial tachycardia is likely contributing. We’ll increase Lasix to help remove fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need a rhythm procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but not now. Anticoagulation would be needed, and it’s too risky with your recent surgery. You’ll follow up with electrophysiology as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Liver biopsy results are back: stage IV fibrosis—severe scarring. Iron is building up in liver cells. This suggests long-term damage, possibly from metabolic or toxic causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that cirrhosis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, essentially. We’ll keep you on Lamivudine and monitor. You’ll need an EGD to check for varices—swollen veins in the stomach—because of the portal hypertension.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The EGD was attempted yesterday, but your stomach wasn’t empty. We repeated it today and found mild portal gastropathy and a small nodule. Biopsy showed no cancer or serious changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this time. We’ll keep you on omeprazole and monitor. The main concern was bleeding risk from varices, which we didn’t see.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugars have been high. The steroids are making it worse. We tried glipizide, but now we’re switching to insulin—Lantus at night and sliding scale during the day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on oral meds before. Will I need insulin forever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. Once the steroids are tapered, we may adjust. But with diabetes and transplant, blood sugar control is critical to healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count dropped, so we reduced CellCept. It can suppress bone marrow. We’re now at 500 mg twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had diarrhea too. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, CellCept can cause that. The dose reduction should help. C. diff test was negative, so it’s likely medication-related.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a paracentesis today—removed 240 cc of fluid. The cell count suggests peritonitis. We’re starting fluconazole while we wait for culture results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Peritonitis? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but we caught it early. The culture grew Candida krusei, a yeast. We’ll switch to micafungin, which works better against this type.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is now 1.2—excellent! The JP drain is out, but we’re keeping Lasix at 40 mg to prevent more fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. But I feel a leak near my incision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, ascites is leaking from the right lower incision. We’ll increase Lasix to 60 mg and monitor. If it continues, we may need to open part of the wound.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound shows the fluid collection is still there. Resistive indices are a bit high in one kidney, but we’re not sure if it’s technical or real. We’ll repeat soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. It could just be how the machine read it. Your urine output and creatinine are stable, which is most important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The leak from your incision is worse. We’ll do another paracentesis to remove fluid and reduce pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We removed 310 cc of fluid yesterday. But the incision is still draining. We’ve decided to partially open it and place a wound VAC to help it heal from the inside out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A vacuum? That sounds intense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s very effective. It reduces fluid buildup and helps new tissue grow. A visiting nurse will change the dressing three times a week at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The VAC is working—output dropped from 380 cc to much less. We’re lowering Lasix back to 20 mg for a few days to balance fluid removal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re placing a PICC line in your left arm so you can get IV micafungin at home for two weeks. Your dialysis access is in both arms, so we’re using the brachial vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that interfere with my dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the PICC is for antibiotics only and won’t affect your fistula. It’ll be removed after treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Urine culture showed yeast, but it’s likely from the treatment. We’re continuing micafungin. Blood cultures are negative—no systemic infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. The VAC output is minimal, and you’re walking independently. Home health will assist with wound care and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If all goes well, discharge is planned for tomorrow. You’ll need to monitor weight, blood sugar, and blood pressure daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final plan: You’re on tacrolimus, CellCept, and prednisone—we’ve stopped steroids due to blood sugar issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Lantus at night and sliding scale. Check sugars four times a day. Call the clinic if over 200 consistently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the heart and liver?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue carvedilol and amlodipine. Follow up with cardiology and hepatology. The cirrhosis needs monitoring, but your transplant is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the wound?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The VAC stays on. Nurse changes it three times a week. Watch for redness, fever, or increased drainage—call the clinic immediately if any.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. Keep up the good care, and we’ll see you in the clinic next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. Your condition is stable, mental status clear, and you’re walking well. Home health is scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. It’s been a long stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It has. But your kidneys are working, the infection is under control, and the wound is healing. Keep following the instructions closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call the transplant clinic with any concerns. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon.
